accuracy.evidence: Checked the physics against the AQA 7405 model: KE = zeV in the accelerating region, v = √(2zeV/m), t = d/v so t ∝ √(m/z). With d = 1.0 m and V = 2.0 kV, ²⁴Mg⁺ (24 × 1.66×10⁻²⁷ kg) gives 7.89 μs and ²⁶Mg⁺ 8.21 μs, matching the lab readouts. Boron 20/80 gives Ar 10.8; magnesium 79/10/11 gives 24.3; electrospray adds H⁺ so the peak is at M+1; ²⁴Mg²⁺ sits at m/z 12.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the standard slips named in examiner reports: 'same speed' instead of same kinetic energy (step 2 predict and challenge tag), tallest peak arriving first (step 3 predict, feedback 'Height shows abundance'), sorting by mass instead of m/z for 2+ ions (step 4, m9 and challenge tag), time proportional to mass rather than √(m/z) (step 5 guesses of 32 get a specific reply), and forgetting why ionisation is needed (step 1 fires neutral atoms with the gun off).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is a side-on four-stage spectrometer with an electron gun toggle, animated ion dots drifting through a vacuum tube, and a live time-of-flight spectrum whose axis auto-zooms to the sample. Learners tap peaks to label m/z and set a mystery m/z by dragging along the time axis. No other lab in the set simulates a detector trace built ion by ion.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step makes one idea visible: neutral atoms pass the plates unmoved, so nothing reaches the detector; two isotopes race with speed tags after the same push; peak heights build as ions land so abundance is read from height; the 2+ toggle adds a new early peak at half the m/z; and the mystery step forces the square-root link because only m/z 64 lands at twice the ¹⁶O⁺ time.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions come before the action: whether neutral atoms are detected, which isotope wins the race, which boron peak arrives first, where ²⁴Mg²⁺ lands, and which m/z doubles the flight time. Each answer is echoed back after the reveal ('You predicted Earlier, at m/z 12: spot on!') so the learner sees whether the model they held was right.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The challenge alternates numeric 'four times the m/z, how much longer' items with conceptual picks, and every wrong choice is tagged so the feedback names the exact error: 'Time grows with the square root of m/z', 'Height shows abundance, not arrival order', 'Charge divides the mass'. Tested in the iPhone walkthrough: each wrong pick showed its own tagged message before Next.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences in stage order (ionise, accelerate, fly, detect) and define m/z the first time it appears. Equations are kept to the adult text and the lab readouts. On-canvas labels are numbered 1 to 4 and staggered on phones so 'Ionise' and 'Accelerate' never overlap; tick labels read as plain decimals like 5.1 μs.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a fact the items test: the ionisation equations, KE = zeV, the √(m/z) dependence, the detector current, the M+1 electrospray peak and the 2+ halving. The family tip is a concrete same-push race with two balls. There are no generic study tips, praise padding or repeated summaries.

mobile.evidence: Walked through on iPhone 13: every Show me reached a tick within the time limit, the spectrum zooms so peaks 0.16 μs apart are clearly separated, peak taps hit 44 px-wide zones, the section labels wrap into two rows on narrow screens and all buttons sit below the canvas in thumb reach. Lab file is 19.2 KB, under the 20 KB limit.

accessibility.evidence: The canvas has a live aria-label that lists the sample, voltage, charge mode and each peak as 'm/z 24 at 7.89 microseconds, n ions', so the spectrum is readable without sight. All actions have buttons as well as gestures, colours pair with text labels, and axe reports no violations in light or dark theme.
